text: Every day, people film themselves showing how things are done. Cooking. Wiring. Assembling. Repairing machines. Billions of hours of it. Yet AI still can't watch one of those videos, and come away with a skill it can check.
This is Eye-doss. Show it a task once, and it compiles the video into a program that checks the work.

It watches eight seconds at a time with Muse Spark. Muse Wonder compiles what it saw into steps, the order they really need, amounts you can change, and a visual contract for every step. SAM 3.1 outlines what each contract is about.
Then it watches live. Point any camera at the work, and it knows which step you're on, tells you what comes next, and checks each step against the video.
Today's AI assistants can see what you see, and answer when you ask. Eye-doss knows what should happen next, and speaks up the moment something goes wrong, before you think to ask.
Here, a technician opens an electrical cabinet without switching off the power. Eye-doss flags it while it's happening.
Here, a cook forgets the olive oil. Before it raises an alert, Eye-doss looks back, the way a person would. Then it names the step that was skipped.
And it's open-ended. A graphics card, a stick of RAM, a kitchen, an electrical cabinet. Anything you can film. One video in. A checkable skill out.

And it doesn't stop at people. The same program drives a robot arm, shown the task once, checking every step through its cameras. Knock its work over, and it notices, and rebuilds. With the checks off, the arm says it's done, next to a broken stack.
Built on Meta's models. Muse Spark watches. Muse Wonder compiles. SAM 3.1 outlines. Muse Image draws each skill. And Muse Spark Open can watch on open weights.
Prompting is how we talk to AI. Showing is how we'll teach it. This is Eye-doss.
